about: Real people who lived or worked in Kowloon Walled City (九龍城寨), each from a published source in the repo. This file is separate from the rooms (data/room_uses.json): linked_facts gives the ids of data/room_research.json for the places where each person lived or worked. nameZh is given only where a source prints the Chinese name. in_dec_1986 is true if the source shows the person in the City in December 1986, false if it shows that they were not, and null if the source gives no date.

people.name: Lam Mei Kwong
people.story: Lam Mei Kwong was a dentist in the Walled City. He arrived in the City in 1949. A photo shows him in his dental clinic at 4A Lung Shing Road (龍城路). The caption calls the clinic spacious by Walled City standards. He occupied that address almost continuously from 1949. His dental equipment appeared to date from the same period. The caption says that it was possibly imported second-hand from Japan. The book's map of the late 1980s lists him as a retired dentist, at number 19. The book has no interview with him. Only the photo caption on page 11 and the map index tell his story.

people.name: Yau Lap Cheong
people.story: Yau Lap Cheong came from Chiu Yeung, in China, in 1928, at the age of 20. He lived near and in the Walled City from then until 1990. He first worked as a foreman in a clothing factory. Then a friend handed him a business that sold cigarettes to gamblers. He took over a store and rented its space of about 70 square feet for $6 a month. His brothers joined him. The street had a dance hall, gambling dens and opium dens. The store was open 24 hours a day and used gaslights. His younger brother gambled and sold heroin for a time. Yau quit the store five or six years before the interview of about 1990. He then lived alone in a one-room flat with no windows. He rarely went out and listened to Cantonese opera on the radio. He also owned a fifth-floor flat that paid him $1000 a month in rent. He moved out in 1990, in the first phase of the clearance.

people.home: a one-room flat of no more than about 120 sq ft, with a tiny kitchen and no windows; he also owned a fifth-floor flat that he let
people.work: a rented store of about 70 sq ft in the City (street not named), until about 1984; earlier a foreman in a clothing factory

people.name: Ho Chi Kam
people.story: Ho Chi Kam was a barber. He read about a flat in the Sing Pao Daily News (成報) and bought it. He moved in at the start of 1974. The flat was on Tung Tau Tsuen Road (東頭村道), thus he had no reason to go inside the City. The book says that he lived in the City long before 1985. Before 1985 he worked as a barber for other people. Then a friend offered him the barber's shop at 10 Tai Chang Street (大井街). He borrowed money and took it over in 1985. After that he came into the City every day. The shop stood near the only Government standpipe inside the City. He and his wife both worked there. Most customers were local residents, and the shop was cheaper than barbers outside. When the City was to be demolished, he went back to work for others. He came to the shop only on Wednesdays, his day off. The shop closed in 1991.

people.name: Wong Yu Ming
people.story: Wong Yu Ming was born in 1930. He studied medicine in China. He learnt dentistry and herbal medicine from his father, a dentist, and by his own study. The Communist Party said that he had bad thoughts. Thus he left Chiu Chow (潮州) for Hong Kong in the late 1950s. He came alone, and his wife and children followed. After a few months he rented premises on Lung Shing Road (龍城路) and opened a dental clinic. He bought the premises a year later. He extracted teeth, did fillings and made false teeth. He often made dentures under contract for registered dentists outside the City. Once he had three employees, but by the interview they had left. His wife, Cheung Mei, learnt the trade from him and was his dental assistant. He worked and lived in the clinic 24 hours a day. His seven children lived with their mother in her flat elsewhere. He felt lonely.

people.name: Hui Kwong
people.story: Hui Kwong came from Malaya. As a young man he went to China to support the war against Japan. A few years after 1945 he came to Hong Kong, but he had no valid passport. He then ran a travel agency in China and married at 30. When private businesses closed, he got out to Macau. In 1965 he brought his wife and daughter to Hong Kong. Life was hard, and the family found a cheaper place in the Walled City. The book's introduction says that he lived in the City from 1961. In the 1970s he worked a machine that made plastic goods. He spent 10 years with the Kai Fong Association (九龍城砦街坊福利事業促進委員會). He was a volunteer at first, then part-time staff and treasurer. He left a few months before the announcement of the demolition. In 1991, at 75, he still played in the Chiu Chow Music Club. Its members played Chiu Chow (潮州) music.

people.name: Chau Pak
people.story: Chau Pak was a storekeeper in the Walled City. The book names him only in the index of its map. Anna Dalgliesh drew the map in 1992. The index gives no page number for him. The repo has no interview or caption about him. The map shows the City in the late 1980s, at about the time of the clearance announcement. It marks his place as number 5, beside number 29, the Salvation Army Kindergarten. The repo's facts place his store on Lung Chun Back Road, but that is a guess from the map. The book says that the map is not entirely accurate. The sources give nothing about his home, his family or his years in the City.

people.name: Jetly Chau Sau Yee
people.story: Jetly Chau Sau Yee was born in Chiu Chow (潮州) and came to Hong Kong at six. In 1968, at 14, he left school to help his father in the family bakery. Their first shop, on Tung Tau Tsuen Road (東頭村道) in Wong Tai Sin (黃大仙), was demolished. A friend then told them about a new building in the Walled City. The Kai Fong Association (九龍城砦街坊福利事業促進委員會) prepared the purchase agreement for a fee of $200. The family bought the shop before they heard of any plan to demolish the City. The shop was on Sai Shing (West City) Road (西城路), and he called it the cleanest alley. He paid $100 a month for well-water. The shop made several hundred steamed and baked cakes a day for shops, temples, noodle shops and Chiu Chow families. At New Year they worked for several days without a stop. After the clearance was announced in 1987, foreign tour groups often stopped at the shop. He worried about the clearance because a new shop outside the City had to meet licence standards.

people.work: his Chiu Chow cake shop in a new building on Sai Shing (West City) Road

people.name: Lau Yeung Yin
people.story: Lau Yeung Yin was born in the Walled City, one of 12 children. His father ran a weaving factory on Lung Chun Back Road (龍津後街). The family lived in the factory. There were no beds, so they moved the yarn aside to make space to sleep. In the early 1960s his father was treasurer of the Kai Fong Association (九龍城砦街坊福利事業促進委員會). Lau left school before the Middle Three examinations. He worked as a tailor's apprentice, then in a rattan shop on Hong Kong Island. Later he worked in his father's factory, which made fabric for gloves. In 1982 he took over the family business in a small factory on Sai Shing (West City) Road (西城路). His sister lent him the money for it. Six people worked there, his wife among them. Business slowed in 1985 and 1986, because customers took their orders to mainland China. The family had a public housing unit in Tai Po but rarely slept there. He expected about $103,000 in compensation for the factory.

people.name: Ng Kam Mui
people.story: Ng Kam Mui's parents moved from Hong Kong Island to the Walled City in the 1960s and opened a café. Her mother was Chiu Chow (潮州). Ng lived or worked at the Chung Fat Café on Tung Tau Tsuen Road (東頭村道) for nearly 30 years. As a child she fetched water from taps at each end of the street and bathed there. After primary school she lived and worked in the City. Her father died young, and her mother fought hard to keep the café. In the 1970s the old building came down, and an 11-storey building went up. The family got two storeys in it and about $7000 for nine months of closure. The café sold tea, coffee, congee and rice from 9 a.m. until late at night. Taxi drivers often came there. She rarely went into the inner City and stayed on its outer edge, where the café was. Later she worked elsewhere in Hong Kong. She asked the Government for $5 million in compensation to buy her mother a flat. The café closed in 1991.

people.name: Lee Yu Chun
people.story: Lee Yu Chun worked in her family's candy business from its start in 1964, when she was not yet 10. Her father started the business, called Chui Fung, in Sham Shui Po. The family later moved to Tsz Wan Shan. In 1967 her father found premises in the Walled City. The family rented two floors of a cottage there but still lived in Tsz Wan Shan. Lee later came to live in the City as well. In the early 1970s the factory moved to 12 Sai Shing (West City) Road (西城路). The family rented it at first and later bought it for $40,000. Lee, her two brothers and her 70-year-old grandmother shared the work. Neighbourhood teenagers wrapped the sweets for 40 cents a pound. Lee's own children helped in the alley after school. Work started at 7 a.m., and the wrapping went on until 9 p.m. About ten years before the interview, she also worked in an electronics factory. She hoped to set up the factory again outside the City after the clearance.

people.name: Law Yu Yi
people.story: Law Yu Yi came from Guangdong. The photo caption calls her a former housewife, and the book's map key calls her a retired maid. At the age of 90 she had lived in the City for 28 years. She lived in a small third-floor flat off Lung Chun First Alley. The flat had no windows and was very humid. She shared it with her daughter-in-law, aged 68. The husbands of both women had died. A surviving son lived on a lower floor of the same building. Each day she went to the adjoining park. There she groomed her face carefully in the traditional Chinese way. She also went to the Old People's Centre (老人中心) to drink tea and meet friends.

people.name: Chan Pui Yin
people.story: Chan Pui Yin came to Hong Kong from Chiu Chow (潮州) county in 1947. He first worked for a pottery distributor on Hong Kong Island. In 1955, at the age of 29, he borrowed money and opened a herbal medicine store on Lung Chun Road (龍津道). Business was good, and he bought the place. Later the two-storey building became an 11-storey block. He got two units for the one that he gave up. He sold mainly herbs and also gave medical consultations. His father, a herbal doctor, taught him. His clients came from all over, some from Hong Kong Island. The shop had Chinese medicines on one side and Western toiletries on the other. It opened from 8am to 11pm, but people knocked on his door at night for medicine. He lived high up in the City, with a view of the sea and fresh air. His three sons and a daughter grew up in the City and kept away from drugs.

people.name: Chan Kwong
people.story: Chan Kwong came from Shantou in Chiu Chow (潮州). He came to Hong Kong with his brother in 1948, at the age of 26. He worked as a hawker and in a plastics factory. In 1970 he opened his own factory, Tai Kwong Plastic Factory, in rented premises on Shing Ngam Road in Kowloon City (九龍城). In 1972 he moved it to Tai Chang Street (大井街) in the Walled City. He made hair clips, toys, ornaments and plastic flowers, and then golf balls. First he employed five or six men. Later he used automatic machines, at times 24 hours a day. At one time, 30 or more women worked for him from home. He sold golf balls to the USA, Japan, France and other countries. The 1970s were his best years. In the City he had fewer inspectors and more freedom. At 67 he planned to retire and go back to the mainland. His son and daughter did not want the business.

people.work: Tai Kwong Plastic Factory, Tai Chang Street (大井街), in the Walled City, from 1972; before that, rented premises on Shing Ngam Road, Kowloon City (1970-1972)

people.name: Lee Pui Yuen
people.story: Lee Pui Yuen was a fisherman from Haifeng county. In 1964 he came to Hong Kong by boat with about 10 others. The police held them for three days, but a Christian organisation helped him get out. After a few months in Sham Shui Po, he moved into the Walled City to be with his sister and her family. Four families, more than 20 people, shared about 300 square feet. He had no proper bed space. He worked night shifts in a weaving factory and then had many other jobs. In 1979 he paid about $16,000 to take over a store at 12 Tai Chang Street (大井街). The store had about 700 square feet and sold rice, kerosene, cigarettes and other basic goods. He carried rice and kerosene up 10 or more storeys to customers. The store opened from 8am to midnight. His wife helped him every day. He, his wife and their young son slept behind a partition at the back. The family moved out in 1991.

people.name: Chung Lo Ying
people.story: Chung Lo Ying and her family first lived in Hung Hom. Robbers scared them there, and in 1958 they moved into the Walled City. They agreed with a Chiu Chow (潮州) family, whose wooden hut had burnt down, to build a house on that family's land. The Chungs paid for the building and took the first floor. That place soon became too small, so they rented another first-floor flat. After about 10 years they bought it. Then a construction company offered them a flat in its new building in exchange. She signed the deal at a tea house, without a lawyer. She bought an apartment on the fourth floor of 82 Lung Chun Road (龍津道), overlooking the park. She first rented it for $80 a month and later paid about $40,000 for it. She had 10 children, and six of them arrived after the move into the City. Her children often joined her for dinner. She rarely locked the door. She did not want the City demolished.

people.name: Chung Yuk Yee
people.story: Chung Yuk Yee was a daughter of Chung Lo Ying. She was born in the Walled City in 1961 and lived there until the clearance in 1991. As a girl she walked the bigger alleys past little houses and working wells. Once she went to a big temple with her mother. The City had no real drains, so every morning the family went to the public lavatories at Tung Tau village (東頭村). Later she married. She lived with her husband, son and daughter in her mother's building, but on the north side. Their flat had no windows, fresh air or view. It was only 230 square feet, with a thin wooden partition between two rooms. All four slept in the bedroom. Family and friends played mahjong in the living room. She helped with the cooking at her mother's flat. She bathed her children in murky water from a rooftop tank. Once a rat ran over her baby daughter's bed.

people.home: a windowless flat of 230 square feet, facing north, in the same building as her mother's flat (82 Lung Chun Road (龍津道))

people.name: Cheng San
people.story: Cheng San was a seaman. At the end of 1967, at about 40, he came back to live in Hong Kong, on the Ngau Tau Kok housing estate. He had six children. He knew no trade, so on a relative's advice he started to make rulers. He first rented a factory on Ko Shan Road. In 1968 he moved to bigger, cheaper premises of about 600 square feet on Tai Chang Street (大井街) in the Walled City. He sawed wood from Borneo by machine and painted the rulers. His daughter printed the measurements upstairs. He once had seven or eight workers and sold to Singapore and Malaysia. Later he worked alone, mostly for local and Macau buyers. He often worked from about 10am until midnight or later. He slept in the factory every night to keep drug addicts from stealing. His wife delivered rulers, and his sons carried the wood. He joined a local association that objected to low compensation. He moved out in 1990.

people.name: Hui Tung Choy
people.story: Hui Tung Choy came to Hong Kong in 1947 to live with his aunt. He was 16, and his parents had died. He grew up in Sun Hui, Guangdong, and had only primary schooling. He learned noodle making with his cousin. Then he opened his own noodle-making place with a friend. His noodle factory at the back of 2 Kwong Ming Street (光明街) opened in 1965. The room was barely 200 square feet and had no windows. Air came in only through the narrow door to the street. He chose the City because rents were low and he needed no licence. At its height in 1980, the business had five workers and made about 1000 noodle discs a day. Later his partner became ill and left, and Hui worked alone. The family owned a flat higher up in the same building. But they cooked and showered in the factory. His two daughters did their homework on the flour-covered work bench. In 1992 he was married with two young daughters. He saw more rats and cockroaches as neighbours moved away.

people.home: A flat on a higher floor of the same building as the factory, 2 Kwong Ming Street; earlier Sai Tau village (pulled down in 1985)
people.work: His noodle factory at the back of 2 Kwong Ming Street, barely 200 square feet, with a door on to Kwong Ming Street

people.name: Chan Hip Ping
people.story: Chan Hip Ping worked for the Kowloon Walled City Kai Fong Association (九龍城寨街坊福利會). The Association started on 1 May 1963 to serve the residents. As a very young man, Chan boiled water and served at its receptions. From 1966 he was its Vice-President. The Association had its offices on the third floor of 16 Tung Tau Tsuen Road (東頭村道). It cleaned alleys and drains, removed garbage and worked against fires and burglaries. In the 1970s it started to put up road signs and public lights. Later it paid for more than 200 lights. It ran a school from 1968 to 1979. It also took elderly residents on tours, for example to Aberdeen in 1987. The demolition began on 14 January 1987. The Association then called emergency meetings and took the residents' demands to the Government. More than 3000 residents came to its office. At the peak it held nine meetings a day. At the time of the interview, Chan no longer lived in the City. But he still spoke for its community.
people.lived: Helped the Kai Fong Association from its start in 1963; Vice-President from 1966; no longer a resident at the time of the interview
people.work: Kai Fong Association offices, third floor of 16 Tung Tau Tsuen Road

people.name: Law Kim Kwong
people.story: Law Kim Kwong was a baker in the Walled City. He made steamed sweet cakes. The book shows his workshop full of cakes in small bowls, beside sacks of flour. Another photograph shows him with crossed arms beside a lit stove. Once he worked through the night to finish cakes for a Chiu Chow (潮州) festival. He had lived in the City for 20 years. He came from the Chiu Chow area of eastern Guangdong. The Chiu Chow people had their own dialect and culture, different from the Cantonese. They made up more than 70 per cent of the City's population. Chiu Chow settlers squatted in and around the City in the late 1940s. Refugees from the same area followed in the early 1950s. The book gives no interview with Law, only photographs and a caption.
people.lived: Resident in the City for 20 years (at the time of the photograph; the book gives no year)
people.home: In the City (the book gives no address)
people.work: His bakery in the City (the book gives no address)

people.name: Tsin Mu Lam
people.story: Tsin Mu Lam was a China-trained doctor. His father was a traditional herbal doctor in the City in the 1950s and 1960s. Tsin graduated from the Zhongsan Medical School in Guangzhou in 1961 and practised in China. During the Cultural Revolution, in 1969, he was sent down to the countryside near Dongguan for three years. He came back to Hong Kong in 1973. That year he opened his clinic on the second floor of 10 Tung Tau Tsuen Road (東頭村道). He lived there with his wife and son. He had no Commonwealth qualification, so he was unable to practise outside the City. He used both Chinese and Western medicine. He treated about 30 patients a day, mostly from outside the City. He charged $30 to $40, about a third less than doctors on the housing estates. He bought the clinic outright. He was in his 50s at the interview. For the demolition, more than 80 doctors and dentists elected him to a Government sub-committee. After a hard fight, each clinic was to get $340,000. His clinic closed in 1992.
people.lived: 1973 to 1992 (clinic and home); his father practised in the City in the 1950s and 1960s
people.home: The clinic, second floor of 10 Tung Tau Tsuen Road, with his wife and son
people.work: His clinic, second floor of 10 Tung Tau Tsuen Road; also company doctor for a factory on Tsing Yi

people.name: Chan Wai Shui
people.story: Chan Wai Shui came to Hong Kong from China in 1947, at the age of 18. He learned the noodle business from his uncle. His old premises in Wang Tau Hom were demolished for the MTR. Thus in 1979 he bought a factory on Lo Yan Street (老人街) for $200,000. Prices outside the Walled City were too high for his small business. He registered the purchase with the Welfare Association and needed no licences. At first there was no electricity, so he arranged for cables. Four partners from before the move worked there about nine hours a day from 8am. His co-workers included Mr Shum and Kwan Tsin On. They made egg noodles and won tun pastry from about 10 bags of flour a day. They delivered by car every day to 40 or 50 regular customers. Chan did not live in the City and seldom slept in the factory. He came only to earn a living. He ran the factory for more than 10 years. He was not sure that the compensation was enough for a new factory.
people.lived: Worked in the City from 1979 for more than 10 years; did not live in the City
people.work: His noodle factory on Lo Yan Street

people.name: Wong Hoi Ming
people.story: Wong Hoi Ming was born in 1920 in the Chiu Chow (潮州) region of Guangdong Province. He learned medicine and kung fu in Thailand and later studied under masters in Chiu Chow. In 1949 he fled to Hong Kong alone and left his wife and family in China. He practised medicine on Hong Kong Island. When his building there was demolished, he moved to the Walled City. He knew the City already because he taught martial arts there. He lived and saw patients in one small apartment with no sunlight. The rent was first $150 a month; later he bought the place. He treated rheumatism, fight injuries and back problems with heated cups, herbal poultices, massage and hot herbal medicines. He had no fixed fees. For a time he let people play mahjong at two tables in the room. He shared a bathroom outside, cooked his own food, and ate with a friend from upstairs. At the clearance he expected about $140,000 for the flat.
people.lived: no years given: from his move from Hong Kong Island until the clearance

people.name: To Gui Bon
people.story: To Gui Bon was born in 1937. He worked in the rubber business before he moved to the City. He was also once a driver of private cars, and he moved to the City when that work became illegal. For about 25 years he made rubber plungers in a small factory on Lung Chun Back Road (龍津後街). At first the site was a two-storey stone house, and he lived on the floor above the factory. When the stone house came down for a new building, he moved next door for a while. At the time of the interview he lived nearby and went home to eat. He worked long hours, sometimes until 2 or 3 a.m. His press had no safety grill, so he worked with extra care. He also made shuttlecocks and sink stoppers. In the 1980s the business grew and made $20,000 to $30,000 a month. He once had a couple of employees, but only one assistant stayed. After the clearance announcement, his business dropped. He had two young children.
people.lived: about 25 years of work in the City ('more than 20 years' at one spot), until the clearance
people.home: nearby his factory; earlier, the first floor above the factory

people.name: Cheng Koon Yiu
people.story: Cheng Koon Yiu came to Hong Kong with his family in 1948, at the age of five. The family lived near the Walled City. He went to Chung San, a private school on Lung Chun Road (龍津路) inside the City. At 14 he became an apprentice to a relative who was a dentist. He lived on the first floor above the clinic. After his apprenticeship he worked in a factory and then in a clinic in the New Territories. In 1963 he came back to the City to assist a friend. About four years later he set up his own clinic. Later he rented a room from his teacher, who still practised nearby. Many patients came from outside because prices in the City were lower. He earned about $10,000 a month, and his wife helped him. The rent rose step by step from $450 and reached $2000 in 1987. His family, with two girls and a boy, moved into the clinic and slept on the floor.
people.lived: school in the City from about age 8 or 9; dental apprentice from age 14; in the City again from 1963 until the clearance
people.home: in his clinic, with his wife, two daughters and a son; earlier a bigger place in the City; as an apprentice, the first floor above his master's clinic

people.name: Jackie Pullinger
people.story: Jackie Pullinger was a foreign missionary who worked in the Walled City. She did not live there. Mrs Donnithorne, the wife of Hong Kong's archdeacon, first introduced her to the City. In 1973 she set up 'The Well', a meeting place of the St Stephen's Society. Most of its congregation were drug addicts who wanted to give up heroin. Daily prayer there used healing hands, hymns and open confession to God. The programme claimed considerable success compared with Government programmes. It took her years to win the trust of the addicts and the Triads. Some of her first recruits were Triad members who wanted to stop taking drugs. Local and foreign volunteers helped her, and many stayed for several years. Wong Wai Chung, a former addict, first met her in the 1980s in the Walled City youth centre. Shortly after the clearance announcement, she moved to Mongkok and set up a similar programme there.
people.lived: worked in the City from 1973 ('The Well') until shortly after the clearance announcement; she did not live there

people.name: Yim Kwok Yuen
people.story: Yim Kwok Yuen was a farmer in Guangdong Province. From 1971 he tried almost every year to sneak into Hong Kong. He arrived in 1978, at the age of 35. He trained for some months in a roast-food shop. Then he worked in his uncle's roasting shop in the Walled City. When his younger brother arrived three years later, he started his own roast-meat business. The book dates his cooked-meat factory on Lo Yan Street (老人街) to 1981. In the interview he said that he rented the workshop three years earlier. He and his brother ran the rented, unlicensed workshop and roasted pork, chicken and goose. He started work at 4 a.m. every day. He sold the meat as an unlicensed hawker in Wong Tai Sin (黃大仙) market. At first he shared a 200-square-foot room in the City with seven other single men. Later he bought two flats in one building in the City. He lived in one with his brother and uncle and rented out the other.
people.lived: from 1978 or soon after (his uncle's roasting shop in the City); his own factory from 1981; until the clearance
people.home: one of his two flats in one building in the City, with his brother and uncle; earlier a 200 sq ft room in the City shared by eight single men

people.name: Lam Leung Po
people.story: Lam Leung Po became a partner in a minced-fish factory in 1983. The factory was in an alley off Tai Chang Street (大井街), close to the one Government standpipe in the City. Before that, the business was just outside the City, in the Sai Tau Tsuen (西頭村) squatter village, until the village came down. Lam joined the business after it moved into the City. The shop measured about 480 square feet. Rent in the City was cheaper, and the hygiene rules gave less trouble. Nobody asked for protection money, and no hygiene inspector ever came. The factory made minced fish, eel dumplings and squidballs. It made about 300 catties of minced fish a day. Five full-time workers worked with Lam and his partner, and a few neighbour ladies made dumplings part-time. Most customers came from outside the City. The factory sold minced fish to over 200 shops.

people.name: Lam Tseng Yat
people.story: Lam Tseng Yat was born in China in 1916. At 10 he came to Hong Kong with his father and four brothers. The family first sold groceries near the old market in Kowloon City, then at the new market on Sha Bo Road. The Japanese demolished that market in the War. In 1947 the family bought a small property at 25 Tai Chang Street (大井街) and opened a store. The two-storey stone hut later became a seven-storey building, but the land stayed with the family. The shop sold rice, peanut oil, cigarettes, alcohol and fruit. At one time it was the largest grocery business in the City. He called it a father and son business, and it never paid protection money. He lived in the City with his wife, and all his children were born there. The family lived on the first and fourth floors. When the children moved out, the family sold those flats and he lived in the shop. He refused the clearance offer of $210,000 and asked for a shop for a shop.

people.name: Simon Wong
people.story: Simon Wong was the officer of the Salvation Army (救世軍) responsible for the Walled City. The Salvation Army began work in the City in 1968. A girl of about seven had asked it for a primary school. It rented a flat for a school and a church. The landlord tore down pictures of Jesus, but later he sold the flat to the Army. The primary school closed because its pupils did not qualify for public examinations. The kindergarten on Lung Chun Back Road (龍津後街) continued for many years. Parents paid no formal fee, but they gave $100 a term if they had the money. It looked for sponsors among foreign groups, and one Austrian gentleman sent over $100,000 each year. At least twice a month, the school took the children to a park outside the City or to Kowloon Park. On Sundays the premises became a chapel for 10 to 20 people. Wong said that the City was a peaceful community in the 1960s and 1970s. After the clearance was announced, reports said that crime increased.
people.lived: Officer responsible for the Walled City at the time of the interview, after the demolition was announced; the Salvation Army worked in the City from 1968

people.name: Reverend Isaac Liu
people.story: Isaac Liu was born in 1935. In 1950 he came to Hong Kong from his native village in China. He did not speak Cantonese, and he often felt lonely. A stranger gave him the gospel in Mandarin, and he became a Christian. He volunteered to preach and studied at a seminary for three years. In that time he began work in the Walled City, with a school in a few rented wooden shacks. In 1960 the mission opened a Gospel Centre in a four-storey building on Lung Shing Road (龍城路). It held a chapel, a clinic for drug addicts and the Tak Shing school, which had more than 420 pupils at its peak. In 1971 the mission moved to the old magistrate's buildings, the Yamen (衙門), at the centre of the City. He began to live in the City in the same year. The school closed in 1978, and in 1979 he started the Old People's Centre (老人中心). It grew to 184 members. The clearance forced him to leave the premises in 1991.

people.name: Kwok Lau Hing
people.story: Kwok Lau Hing never lived in the City itself, but she was a regular visitor to its Old People's Centre (老人中心). In her 30s she and her elder sister left Shanghai Street in Yau Ma Tei. They bought a small flat on the second floor of 5C Sai Tau New Street, a settlement on the outskirts of the City. She owned a half share and rented one of her two rooms out. She worked half days as a cleaner and office woman for the Jardine Airline Company in Central. She earned about $100 a month and assembled toys for extra money. She never dared to go into the Walled City itself. Her husband died and left her with two sons and a daughter. The Government decided to clear the settlement in 1985, and the family moved to the Lok Wah estate. After she retired at 65, she joined the Old People's Centre. There she learnt to write and did handcraft and embroidery. She kept making the journey after she moved to Junk Bay. In 1989 she was 73.

people.name: Yu Hing Wan
people.story: Yu Hing Wan made muslin in the City. Muslin was once a major industry there, before synthetic materials came. At 86 he was still at work, and he was the last muslin maker in the City. Like most factory owners in the City, he chose his site on Lung Chun Road (龍津道) for its cheap rent. He needed space for large machinery and for stored cloth. He felt that outside the City the business was not viable, and that there he was not able to own a factory. He lived in the City for 18 years. He came from the Hakka community of Guangdong province. Thus he was in a minority among the mainly Chiu Chow (潮州) population of the City. His factory was neat and clean. But after long years of hard work, the noise of the old machines and the lack of ventilation hurt him most. The photographs show him at a large machine and with long rolls of white cloth.

people.name: Chan Kwan Leung
people.story: Chan Kwan Leung grew up in the first resettlement estates at Shek Kip Mei, and later in the New Territories. His parents were teachers. At 24 he worked for the Hong Kong Telephone Company and left his parents' house. In 1981 he moved into the Walled City, where he bought a flat for $68,000. He met his wife there. Her mother gave him a pigeon, and soon he kept many birds. In about 1981 or 1982 he built cages on the roof of his building. The owner of the flat below agreed, but other people complained. He quit his job to care for the birds, and at one stage he had more than 1000. He did not tell his wife or his parents. He bought and sold pigeons and started a pigeon-racing club with friends. The club raced birds from Shanghai and other places in China. In January 1987 the Housing Department registered him as a resident and announced the clearance. On that day he decided to close his pigeon business.
